newsitem.title: USA: Midwest rebounds from GM strike - Chicago Fed.
newsitem.headline: Midwest rebounds from GM strike - Chicago Fed.

text.p: An official from the Chicago Federal Reserve Bank said the Midwest economy rebounded in December as it continued to recover from the effects of a recent General Motors Corp strike.
Robert Schnorbus, senior economist and assistant vice president at the Chicago Fed, said, "we're still getting a rebound from the strike effects that were occurring in September and October."
Schnorbus was speaking to Reuters Financial Television after the Chicago Fed released its monthly report on area manufacturing on Tuesday morning.
The Chicago Fed Midwest Manufacturing Index rose 1.0 percent to 124.4 in December.
The gain represented a very strong performance for the Midwest manufacturing sector but did not necessarily reflect underlying strength in the regional economy, Schnorbus said.
Auto production, a key component of the index, rose a meager 0.1 percent in December.
But Schnorbus said auto production in the first half of 1997 should be "reasonably strong," particularly in the Midwest.
That strength would add to the steel and machinery sectors of the economy, he said. "It's going to pull steel (and) probably machinery up for a short period of time," the economist said.
Asked about inflation, Schnorbus said wage increases appear to be more widespread now in the Midwest.
"The reports we're getting from our region ... (show) a widening number of reports of wage increases," he said.
"It's too early to over-interpret the reports we're getting on wage increases, but I think it's something that has to be seriously monitored," he added.
The economist said shifts in prices should be gradual in either direction.
"No one is seriously expecting prices or wages to suddenly explode on the market," Schnorbus said. "It's going to be a gradual, creeping increase or decrease."
